newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan urges keeping Fed's supervisory role.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan urges keeping Fed's supervisory role.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Wednesday that it was important for the Fed to maintain its supervisory role over banks as part of its ability to protect the financial system in times of crises.

In testimony before a House Banking subcommittee, Greenspan warned that financial crises spread more rapidly than in the past and that it was necessary for the Fed to maintain regulatory control of large banks so that it can intercede at times when it appeared the financial system was going to become unstable.
"There are compelling reasons why the central bank of the United States -- the Federal Reserve -- should continue to be involved in the supervision of banks," Greenspan said in prepared testimony.

"The supervisory activities of the Federal Reserve, for example, have benefited from its economic stabilization responsibilities and its recognition that safety and soundness goals for banks must be evaluated jointly with its responsibilities for stability and growth of the economy."

Greenspan noted that while the U.S. financial system has been characterized by innovation and rapid change with significant benefits to the economy, one of the consequences of such a dynamic system was that it produced "episodes of stress."

He detailed a series of problems that has shaken the system, including the international debt crisis, a major stock market crash, problems in the junk bond market and the "virtual failure" of the savings and loan industry as examples.

Greenspan said the objective of the central bank in crisis management was to contain financial losses and prevent a contagious loss of confidence so that difficulties at one institution do not spread more rapidly to others.

He said the ability of the Fed to do this required "in-depth knowledge of how institutions of various sizes and other characteristics are likely to behave and what resources are available to them in the event of severe financial stress."

He also noted that the payment and settlement systems of the U.S., including the Fed wire, are crucial and "arguably the linchpin" of the international system of payments that relies on the dollar as the major international currency for trade and finance.
Greenspan said it was the Fed board's view that the current supervisory authority was adequate for the current structure of the financial system.
However, he said that if changes are made in the future the board believes that Congress would need to change the supervisory structure of the central bank so it could carry out its responsibilities.
Greenspan also defended the use of consolidated umbrella supervision as it presently operates.
"Risks managed on a consolidated basis cannot be reviewed on an individual legal entity basis by different supervisors," Greenspan maintained.
He said that for foreign and U.S. banking organizations, "retreat from consolidated supervision would, the board believes, be a significant step backwards."
But he said it was necessary to be careful that such supervision did not inadvertently "so hamper the decision making process of banking organizations as to render them ineffectual."

Greenspan repeated the board's position that banks inherently through their deposit insurance have a subsidy, and that it would be undesirable that banks conducting new activities through subsidiaries "inadvertently extend that subsidy."

He noted that banks with troubled loan portfolios in the 1980s and 1990s benefited substantially by having deposit liabilities guaranteed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp as well as the use of the Fed's discount window.
"For some it meant the difference between survival and failure," he said.

Looking to the future, Greenspan said, "We must be very careful that in the name of free market efficiency we do not countenance greater powers and profits subsidized directly or indirectly by government.
